paragraphs: This paper develops an evaluation framework for face forgery detection using models that combine vision and language. Its central concern is that deciding whether a face is fake does not adequately test whether a model can identify and describe manipulated regions. The authors therefore treat detection as visual question answering, including questions whose answers can name several manipulated areas.

The evaluation proceeds through increasingly expressive tasks. First, models make binary judgments under different prompts, revealing sensitivity to instructions. Next, they identify manipulation areas using multiple-choice questions. Then they answer open-ended questions, with several matching strategies used to connect generated text to multiple detection labels. A final qualitative assessment examines the responses themselves.

The benchmark compares popular models across seven datasets. Its contribution is a structured way to assess binary decisions, localized detection, and free-form explanations together. This matters because the ability to produce an informative answer requires evaluation beyond a real-or-fake label, including how generated descriptions are interpreted and scored.
neurips-2024-a-hitchhiker-s-guide-to-fin.tldr: A staged benchmark evaluates whether vision-language models can detect face forgeries and describe multiple manipulated regions.

paragraphs: Learning rate warmup starts training with smaller steps before increasing their size. This paper investigates why that practice helps, focusing on small-scale GPT training with AdamW and Lion. The authors argue that warmup restrains unusually large early optimizer updates, making the size of the actual weight change the central quantity to understand.

They examine update size from several perspectives: the overall magnitude of a weight change, how much it rotates the weight direction, and how it changes the network's internal representations. These perspectives distinguish a numerically large step from one that substantially changes how the model behaves. Their analysis finds that warmup counteracts large angular changes and a limited critical batch size early in training.

The authors then modify the optimizer to normalize updates directly using these measurements. In the studied setting, this substantially reduces or eliminates the need for warmup. The finding suggests that explicitly controlling early updates can replace a schedule that controls them indirectly through the learning rate.
neurips-2024-analyzing-reducing-the-need.tldr: In small-scale GPT training, directly normalizing optimizer updates can substantially reduce or eliminate learning rate warmup.

paragraphs: CARE provides a standardized way to evaluate machine learning methods for identifying enzyme functions. Enzymes are proteins that catalyze chemical reactions, and the benchmark connects their sequences and associated reactions to enzyme commission, or EC, numbers. Its motivation is that methods for predicting function from sequence need shared evaluation tasks and datasets.

The suite separates two questions. Classification asks which EC number belongs to a protein sequence. Retrieval asks which EC number corresponds to a chemical reaction. For both tasks, the authors design training and testing splits that examine different forms of generalization beyond the training distribution, chosen to reflect relevant practical uses.

CARE includes existing leading methods as classification baselines. For reaction-based retrieval, which the authors identify as a newly formalized task, they introduce Contrastive Reaction-EnzymE Pretraining, or CREEP, and compare it with CLIPZyme. The contribution is both a common testing framework and an initial basis for studying retrieval alongside sequence classification, without treating the two problems as interchangeable.
neurips-2024-care-a-benchmark-suite-for-.tldr: CARE standardizes enzyme classification and reaction-based EC-number retrieval, with evaluation splits designed to test practical forms of generalization.

paragraphs: CAT addresses medical image segmentation, where a model marks the regions belonging to organs or tumors. The authors argue that either text or visual prompts alone can be insufficient for anomalies whose shape, size, and appearance vary substantially. Their approach combines anatomical image information with descriptions enriched by medical knowledge.

The anatomical prompts come from cropped three-dimensional images. Textual prompts provide a complementary source of guidance. Within a query-based architecture, prompt queries assist segmentation queries in predicting masks. A component called ShareRefiner updates both kinds of queries while keeping the two prompt types disentangled, allowing the model to coordinate their contributions within one framework.

The model is trained using ten public CT datasets and shows superior performance across multiple segmentation tasks. Additional validation on an in-house dataset demonstrates tumor segmentation across several cancer stages. These results support the authors' conclusion that coordinating visual anatomy and medical text is a promising approach for complex segmentation scenarios, especially when the target appearance is highly variable.
neurips-2024-cat-coordinating-anatomical.tldr: CAT combines anatomical image prompts and medically informed text prompts to improve organ and tumor segmentation.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether optimized prompts remain useful when a language model encounters unfamiliar domains. The authors begin with pilot experiments showing two associations: prompts that receive stronger attention in deeper model layers generalize better, and prompts with more stable attention distributions in those layers also generalize better.

They turn these observations into an optimization objective called Concentration. It measures attention directed backward from the token currently being decoded to the prompt tokens. Optimization encourages stronger attention to the prompt while reducing fluctuations in how that attention is distributed. The objective is incorporated into both soft prompt and hard prompt optimization methods.

In experiments involving generalization from multiple source domains, the authors report accuracy improvements of 1.42% for soft prompts and 2.16% for hard prompts over the comparison methods. Performance within the original domains remains satisfactory. The results support using the model's attention to its instructions as an additional training signal when optimizing prompts for unfamiliar domains.
neurips-2024-concentrate-attention-towar.tldr: Encouraging stronger, steadier attention to prompt tokens improves prompt generalization to unfamiliar domains in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Learning related tasks sequentially can help a network reuse knowledge, but can also overwrite earlier learning. This paper separates two kinds of similarity: similarity in input features and similarity in the patterns used to produce outputs. Using a linear teacher-student model with latent structure, the authors analyze their different effects on transfer and forgetting.

Within that model, highly similar inputs paired with dissimilar readouts are catastrophic for both transfer and retention. The reverse combination is relatively benign. The analysis also distinguishes interventions: task-dependent activity gating improves retention at the cost of transfer, whereas task-dependent plasticity gating changes neither in the over-parameterized limit.

Regularization using the Fisher information metric improves retention without sacrificing transfer, regardless of task similarity in the analysis. Its diagonal approximation and Euclidean regularization are less robust to similarity. Experiments on a permuted MNIST task with latent variables produce consistent findings. The work therefore explains why calling tasks simply similar can conceal very different continual-learning challenges.
neurips-2024-disentangling-and-mitigatin.tldr: A structured linear analysis shows how input and output similarity interact to drive transfer and forgetting in continual learning.

paragraphs: Feints are deceptive actions that help a player gain advantages in timing or position against an opponent. This paper gives them a formal treatment at both the level of individual actions and the level of game strategy. The aim is to make these behaviors concrete enough to generate, implement, and evaluate in competitive multiplayer settings.

The proposed system automatically generates feint behaviors using palindrome-directed templates. A Dual-Behavior Model combines them into meaningful sequences. The authors also formalize how feints affect temporal advantages, spatial advantages, and the combination of both, connecting the generated actions to their strategic role rather than evaluating isolated movements alone.

The implementation is designed to fit existing multi-agent reinforcement learning frameworks. Experiments report substantial improvements in game rewards and greater diversity in multiplayer games, with negligible additional time costs. These findings support treating feints as an explicit component of learned competitive behavior and provide a unified framework for investigating their effects on game outcomes.
neurips-2024-feint-behaviors-and-strateg.tldr: A formal framework generates and integrates feints into multi-agent learning, improving rewards and game diversity with negligible reported time overhead.

paragraphs: This paper aims to make vision-language models more resistant to adversarial image changes that are difficult to perceive. Earlier approaches align attacked visual features with text supervision, but the authors identify costly adaptation, inadequate text supervision, and uncontrolled generalization on natural examples as obstacles. They propose adapting prompts using limited training data.

The framework learns its text supervision directly from adversarial examples, so the text guidance is tailored to the attacked visual features. Its training objective combines two goals: making features across the visual and textual modalities more consistent, while encouraging features within an individual modality to distinguish natural examples from adversarial ones.

The reported result is stronger cross-modal adversarial alignment and robustness matching leading zero-shot adversarial methods with only 1% of the training data. The contribution is therefore a way to learn useful adversarial supervision through prompts with much less data. The result concerns the evaluated robustness setting rather than establishing resistance to every possible image perturbation.
neurips-2024-few-shot-adversarial-prompt.tldr: Learning adversarially informed prompts matches leading zero-shot robustness results using only 1% of the training data.

paragraphs: This paper helps reinforcement learning agents pursue distant goals by deriving useful intermediate goals. Its goal-reducer uses a loop-removal technique to extract high-quality subgoals from stored experience in a replay buffer. The mechanism does not require prior global knowledge of the environment, making previously collected experience the basis for breaking down a larger objective.

In simulations, the goal-reducer integrates with Deep Q-learning and Soft Actor-Critic. It accelerates performance relative to their standard versions in tasks with discrete and continuous actions, including grid navigation and robotic arm manipulation. In a navigation task, combining the reducer with a local policy, without iterative training, also outperforms its integrated deep reinforcement learning counterparts.

The authors additionally compare the model with human behavior and brain activity during treasure hunting. They find corresponding representational patterns in model components and brain regions, particularly the vmPFC and basal ganglia. These similarities suggest that humans may use a related computational framework for goal-directed behavior; they do not establish that the mechanisms are identical.
neurips-2024-goal-reduction-with-loop-re.tldr: A loop-removal goal-reducer improves reinforcement learning and exhibits representational similarities to human brain activity during goal-directed problem solving.

paragraphs: HyperLogic addresses a tension in learning interpretable if-then rules with neural networks. Sparse, shallow networks can be trained with standard gradient methods and then translated into global rule sets. However, keeping the network easy to interpret can restrict its depth, width, and flexibility, limiting the patterns it can express.

The proposed framework uses a hypernetwork to generate the weights of the main network. This allows HyperLogic to produce multiple diverse rule sets, each capturing different patterns in the data. The approach expands the range of rules the system can learn while preserving the ability to express its learned behavior through interpretable logical rules.

The authors theoretically examine approximation error and generalization under sparsity and diversity regularization. These two forms of regularization address how compact the learned rules are and how varied the resulting sets can be. Experiments on real data show more diverse, accurate, and concise rules, supporting the use of generated network weights to increase flexibility in interpretable rule learning.
neurips-2024-hyperlogic-enhancing-divers.tldr: HyperLogic uses hypernetworks to generate diverse interpretable rule sets, improving rule accuracy and conciseness in real-data experiments.

paragraphs: This paper compresses the key and value cache used during language model inference. As requests are batched together or contexts and models grow, this cache can dominate GPU memory and constrain throughput. Existing quantization methods struggle when pushed to very few bits, motivating a closer look at how cached information is encoded.

The authors find that different channels of key and value activations are strongly dependent. Their combined information content grows more slowly than the sum of the information in each channel considered separately. Coupled Quantization exploits this structure by encoding groups of channels together, instead of treating each channel independently.

Experiments show favorable preservation of model quality compared with existing baselines and inference throughput improvements of 1.4–3.5 times relative to an uncompressed baseline. The authors also report reasonable quality preservation with a one-bit KV cache. The key finding is that accounting for dependencies between channels can make extremely compact cache representations more effective than independent quantization.
neurips-2024-kv-cache-is-1-bit-per-chann.tldr: Coupled Quantization jointly compresses dependent KV-cache channels, improving throughput and reasonably preserving model quality down to one bit.

paragraphs: LT-Defense detects backdoors in language models by examining effects left by poisoned training data. Existing defenses search for the triggers that activate malicious behavior, which can become expensive when there are many possibilities. The authors instead observe a long-tailed effect in poisoned models, accompanied by a decision-boundary shift toward the attacker's targets.

The method uses a small collection of clean examples and two metrics to distinguish features associated with a backdoor. This makes the observed model behavior, rather than a search over possible triggers, the basis for detection. After identifying a backdoored model, the framework also provides test-time backdoor freezing and prediction of the attack target.

Experiments support both detection accuracy and efficiency. In task-agnostic scenarios, the authors report 98% accuracy across 1,440 models while using less than 1% of the time required by leading comparison solutions. The result indicates that the poisoning effect can provide a practical detection signal without incurring the cost of trigger search.
neurips-2024-lt-defense-searching-free-b.tldr: LT-Defense detects language-model backdoors through poisoning-induced effects, avoiding trigger searches and sharply reducing reported detection time.

paragraphs: This paper studies how reinforcement learning can learn a starting point that adapts effectively across tasks. The proposed BO-MRL framework uses bilevel optimization: one level learns the shared meta-prior, while another adapts a policy to a particular task. Task adaptation performs multiple policy-optimization steps using data collected on a single occasion.

The theoretical contribution is an upper bound on the expected gap between the adapted policy and each task's own optimum. Averaging this gap over the task distribution evaluates how well the learned starting point supports adaptation across that distribution. This comparison ties generalization to task-specific optimal performance rather than merely measuring improvement from the initial policy.

The authors empirically validate their derived bounds and report stronger effectiveness than benchmark methods. Together, the analysis and experiments connect a concrete adaptation procedure with a measure of how close its results come to task optima. The guarantee concerns expected performance over the task distribution, rather than an unconditional claim about every individual task.
neurips-2024-meta-reinforcement-learning.tldr: BO-MRL learns a reusable policy prior and bounds the expected gap between task-adapted policies and their task-specific optima.

paragraphs: This paper proposes estimating mutual information by changing the distribution on which the estimation problem is carried out. Mutual information concerns the information shared between variables. Instead of working only with the original data distribution, the authors introduce a family of estimators based on normalizing flows that map the data to a target distribution.

The target is chosen to make mutual information easier to estimate. The authors also investigate target distributions whose mutual information has a known closed-form expression, allowing the target-side calculation to use an explicit formula. The central idea is to move the statistical calculation into a more manageable representation while retaining a connection to the original problem.

The paper supplies theoretical guarantees that the procedure yields mutual information estimates for the original data. Experiments with high-dimensional data illustrate practical advantages of the approach. The combination matters because an easier calculation after transformation is useful only when it remains informative about the quantity sought before transformation.
neurips-2024-mutual-information-estimati.tldr: Normalizing flows transform data into distributions where mutual information is easier to estimate, with guarantees connecting estimates to the original data.

paragraphs: NeuralSolver is designed to learn algorithms from small problems and apply them to larger ones. Here, size refers to the size of the observation. The work addresses both problems whose inputs and outputs have matching sizes and problems where those sizes differ, extending the range of tasks handled naturally by a recurrent solver.

Its architecture has a recurrent module that repeatedly processes information at different scales and a processing module that aggregates what has been processed. A curriculum-based training scheme improves extrapolation. These components combine repeated computation, information aggregation, and a structured training progression to support execution on problems larger than those used for learning.

The authors introduce new tasks with differing input and output sizes to evaluate this capability. NeuralSolver consistently outperforms previous leading recurrent solvers on extrapolation to larger problems in the reported evaluations, while training on smaller problems and using fewer parameters than other approaches. The findings connect architectural versatility with improved efficiency in learning computations that transfer across problem sizes.
neurips-2024-neuralsolver-learning-algor.tldr: NeuralSolver learns on smaller problems and more effectively extrapolates to larger ones, including tasks with unequal input and output sizes.

paragraphs: This paper studies goodness-of-fit testing for discrete distributions when observations are spread across multiple servers. The task is to assess whether data agree with a proposed distribution. Unlike a centralized setting, servers cannot freely pool their observations because communication bandwidth or differential privacy requirements restrict the information they can share.

The authors connect this distributed discrete-data problem to existing results for testing the mean of a multivariate Gaussian model. They use Le Cam's theory of statistical equivalence to transfer those results between statistical settings. This provides a route to characterizing the discrete problem through a related problem whose constrained testing behavior has already been analyzed.

The resulting upper and lower minimax bounds match in the regime where each location holds many samples. Upper bounds establish achievable testing performance, while lower bounds establish corresponding worst-case limits. Their agreement identifies optimal performance under the studied bandwidth or privacy constraints. The large local sample regime is central to the scope of this result.
neurips-2024-optimal-private-and-communi.tldr: Matching theoretical bounds characterize distributed discrete goodness-of-fit testing under bandwidth or privacy constraints when local sample sizes are large.

paragraphs: QBB compresses language-model weights through combinations of binary matrices and scaling vectors. Its aim is low-bit computation that removes nearly all multiplications, reducing implementation largely to summations. The motivation is that pushing compression beyond common four-bit methods without large accuracy losses remains difficult, particularly for models below seven billion parameters.

The method first builds an analytical approximation of each weight matrix. Each additional binary matrix and its scaling vector approximate the error left by the preceding approximation. It then refines these components with gradient descent and a progressive learning curriculum, minimizing the distance between the reconstructed weights and the original weights.

A final calibration stage optimizes only the scaling vectors in a student-teacher setup. The teacher supplies both generated text, starting from a random token, and target output scores. This adds input-dependent calibration after the earlier weight-focused stages. Across multiple model families, the authors report results matching or surpassing prior work, establishing strong performance for their summation-based approach.
neurips-2024-qbb-quantization-with-binar.tldr: QBB approximates language-model weights with binary matrices and calibrated scales to achieve competitive low-bit performance using nearly multiplication-free computation.

paragraphs: ReMoDetect detects generated text by exploiting a property shared by many powerful language models: alignment training to produce human-preferred responses. The authors find that aligned models can produce text receiving higher estimated preference scores than human writing. A reward model trained to represent human preferences can therefore provide a detection signal.

The method strengthens that signal with two training schemes. Continual preference fine-tuning encourages the reward model to prefer aligned model outputs even more strongly. A second scheme introduces human-written text rephrased by aligned models. These mixed texts serve as an intermediate preference group, helping the detector learn the boundary between human and generated writing.

Evaluation spans six text domains and twelve aligned language models, with the authors reporting state-of-the-art results. The approach matters because it focuses on a shared training characteristic instead of requiring separate treatment of every generating model. Its finding concerns estimated preferences and detection of aligned outputs, rather than a claim that generated writing is inherently better than human writing.
neurips-2024-remodetect-reward-models-re.tldr: ReMoDetect identifies aligned language-model text using its unusually high reward-model preference scores and further trains that signal for detection.

paragraphs: SolarCube is a benchmark dataset for forecasting solar radiation. Clouds make the amount of sunlight reaching the ground variable, complicating decisions about storage and backup power. The dataset addresses the need for machine-learning-ready information that connects frequent satellite observations with detailed radiation measurements and supports consistent evaluation of forecasting models.

It combines geostationary satellite images, physics-derived solar radiation, and observations from ground monitoring networks. Coverage includes nineteen study areas across North America, South America, Asia, and Oceania. Forecasting tasks include individual monitoring locations and wider areas, with horizons ranging from thirty minutes to six hours and extending to a day ahead or longer.

The authors evaluate forecasting models for both point-based and image-based time series under different testing scenarios. These evaluations establish performance benchmarks alongside the dataset itself. A companion Python library supports generating dataset variations for different needs. The contribution is a shared foundation for comparing forecasts across spatial scales and time horizons using integrated observations.
neurips-2024-solarcube-an-integrative-be.tldr: SolarCube integrates satellite, physics-derived, and ground observations to benchmark solar radiation forecasting across locations, areas, and time horizons.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether model explanations remain stable when inputs are attacked. The authors argue that commonly used numerical distance measures do not align well with human perception of explanation changes. They introduce a metric centered on the top-k salient features, focusing evaluation on the features highlighted as most important.

Their training method, R2ET, uses an efficient regularizer to encourage explanation stability. This responds to the computational expense of adversarial training and the prospect of continually adapting to new attacks. The authors analyze the method through multi-objective optimization and prove numerical and statistical stability of explanations.

They also establish theoretical connections to certified robustness, which they use to justify stability across attacks in their analysis. Experiments covering several data modalities and model architectures show superior stability against stealthy attacks and effective generalization across explanation methods. The contribution combines a different way to assess explanation changes with a training approach and theoretical support for keeping explanations consistent.
neurips-2024-training-for-stable-explana.tldr: R2ET uses an efficient training regularizer and a top-feature stability metric to improve explanation robustness, supported by theory and experiments.

paragraphs: UltraEdit is an automatically generated dataset containing approximately four million examples of editing images from written instructions. The paper focuses on how to produce editing data at scale while improving instruction diversity, image diversity, and support for changes to particular regions. Its contribution is a systematic data-generation approach as well as the resulting dataset.

Instruction generation combines language-model creativity with editing examples provided by human raters. The source images are real photographs or artworks, which the authors report offer greater diversity and less bias than images produced entirely by text-to-image models. Automatically generated region annotations additionally support edits directed at specific parts of an image.

Diffusion-based editing baselines trained on UltraEdit achieve new records on the MagicBrush and Emu-Edit benchmarks. Further analysis confirms the important roles of real image anchors and region-based editing data. These findings indicate that the composition of editing examples, including their source imagery and localized guidance, contributes to the reported performance alongside the dataset's scale.
neurips-2024-ultraedit-instruction-based.tldr: UltraEdit supplies roughly four million instruction-based image edits, using real image anchors and region annotations to improve benchmark performance.

paragraphs: This paper estimates missing phenotype information by incorporating multiple forms of biological data. Such data can enrich patient characterization, but their heterogeneity and imprecision make them difficult to combine effectively. The proposed framework separates biological information and phenotype information into two views instead of treating them as one undifferentiated source.

A graph-based learning framework models each view separately. In the biological view, latent factors reveal relationships among patients. In the phenotype view, patterns of phenotype co-occurrence reveal structure across patients. The model then encodes patients from both perspectives, preserving the distinct kinds of relationships each source contributes.

To reduce the influence of noise and irrelevant biological information, the authors introduce cross-view contrastive knowledge distillation. This transfers useful insights from the biological view to support phenotype imputation. On a real-world biomedical database, the proposed model significantly outperforms leading comparison models. The result supports separating the views during modeling and selectively transferring their information for the specific task of filling in missing phenotypes.
neurips-2024-unified-insights-harnessing.tldr: Separately modeling biological and phenotype relationships, then transferring useful information between them, improves missing-phenotype prediction.

paragraphs: UniSDF reconstructs three-dimensional scenes from two-dimensional images, with particular attention to scenes containing reflections. General reconstruction methods can miss fine geometry and reflective appearance, while methods specialized for reflections can struggle when reflective and non-reflective components coexist. The paper aims to handle these mixed, complex scenes within a general-purpose method.

The authors investigate color representations based on both the camera view and the reflected view. Explicitly blending those representations in three-dimensional space produces more geometrically accurate surfaces, especially reflective ones. They combine this representation with a multi-resolution grid trained from coarse to fine, enabling faster reconstruction than prior methods.

Evaluation covers the object-level DTU and Shiny Blender datasets and the unbounded Mip-NeRF 360 and Ref-NeRF real datasets. The authors report robust reconstruction of large, detailed scenes with reflective surfaces and the best overall performance in their experiments. The findings support coordinating complementary appearance representations to improve geometry while using the grid backbone to accelerate reconstruction.
neurips-2024-unisdf-unifying-neural-repr.tldr: UniSDF blends camera-view and reflected-view representations to reconstruct detailed scenes with reflections more accurately and quickly.

paragraphs: VRSBench is a dataset for training and evaluating vision-language models on remote sensing imagery. The authors identify three shortcomings in existing datasets: narrow focus on individual tasks, insufficient object detail, and inadequate quality control. Their benchmark brings several forms of language supervision together to support broader image understanding.

The dataset contains 29,614 images and an equal number of detailed, human-verified captions. It also includes 52,472 object references and 123,221 question-answer pairs. These annotation types support complementary capabilities: describing an image, locating an object referred to in language, and answering questions about image content.

The authors evaluate leading models on image captioning, visual grounding, and visual question answering using the benchmark. These evaluations provide a common setting for examining multiple capabilities relevant to general-purpose remote sensing models. The main contribution is the combination of detailed captions, object references, and questions within one resource, allowing development and assessment to extend beyond a single narrowly defined task.
neurips-2024-vrsbench-a-versatile-vision.tldr: VRSBench combines captions, object references, and question-answer pairs to evaluate multiple vision-language capabilities on remote sensing images.

paragraphs: This paper develops a policy-optimization algorithm for reinforcement learning under a linear Markov decision process model. It addresses a drawback of an earlier method with rate-optimal regret guarantees: the need for a costly initial phase devoted purely to exploration. The authors describe that phase as difficult to implement in practice.

Their algorithm replaces the exploration warmup with a simple, efficient contraction mechanism. The theoretical goal is to retain rate-optimal regret while improving how the guarantee depends on other problem parameters. Regret tracks the performance shortfall accumulated during learning, so controlling it concerns the cost of learning as well as eventual policy quality.

The resulting guarantees have improved dependence on the decision horizon and the dimension used for function approximation. They apply in two settings: adversarial losses with full-information feedback and stochastic losses with bandit feedback. The contribution is therefore a warmup-free procedure with stronger parameter dependence in these specified linear-MDP settings, preserving the central regret-rate guarantee of the earlier approach.
neurips-2024-warm-up-free-policy-optimiz.tldr: A contraction mechanism removes pure-exploration warmup while retaining rate-optimal regret with improved parameter dependence in two linear-MDP settings.
